n: The scene shifts north. Jabin, king of Hazor — the most powerful city in northern Canaan — rallies other kings against Israel.

f.g: “Jabin” may have been a royal title; another Jabin of Hazor appears in Judges.
A huge city north of the Sea of Galilee.

n: He summons kings from the northern hills, the Jordan valley south of the Sea of Galilee, the lowlands, and the coast near Dor.

f.g: The Sea of Galilee (Kinneret), named perhaps for its harp-like shape.
A Mediterranean port city.

n: A coalition of nearly every people group in Canaan, all the way to the Hivites below Mount Hermon.

f.g: The tall snow-capped mountain at Israel’s northern edge.

n: A massive army, as countless as sand on the seashore, with many horses and chariots — the most advanced military technology of the day.

f.w: as the sand that is upon the sea shore

n: They gather and camp at the waters of Merom to fight Israel.

f.g: Springs or a stream in upper Galilee, location uncertain.

n: God tells Joshua not to fear: by this time tomorrow the enemy will be defeated. Israel must disable the horses and burn the chariots so they would not come to trust in military might.

f.g: Hough = hamstring — cut the leg tendons so horses can’t be used for war.

n: Joshua launches a surprise attack at Merom.

f.g: Without warning — Joshua’s favored tactic.

n: God gives the victory. Israel chases the survivors north to Sidon and east to the valley of Mizpeh.

f.g: Sidon, the chief Phoenician city on the coast.
Possibly “hot waters” or “burning of waters” — a site near the coast.

n: Joshua obeys exactly: he hamstrings the horses and burns the chariots.

f.g: Bade = commanded.

n: Then he turns back and captures Hazor, the head of the alliance, killing its king.

f.w: the head of all those kingdoms
f.g: The leading city of northern Canaan.

n: Hazor is placed under the ban and burned. Archaeologists have found a massive burn layer at Hazor from the late Bronze Age, though its exact date and cause are debated.

f.g: Hazor alone of the northern cities was burned.

n: All the allied cities and kings are taken, as Moses had commanded.

f.w: as Moses the servant of the LORD commanded

n: The cities on their mounds were not burned — Israel would live in them — except Hazor. God had promised houses and cities they did not build.

f.g: Stood on their mounds (tels).

n: Israel kept the plunder and livestock, as God allowed after Jericho.
A key verse: God commanded Moses, Moses commanded Joshua, and Joshua left nothing undone. Faithful obedience passes down the chain of prophetic authority.
A summary of the conquered territory: hills, the Negev, Goshen, the lowlands, the Arabah, and the hill country of Israel.

f.g: The Arabah — the Jordan rift valley.

n: From Mount Halak in the south near Edom (Seir) to Baal-gad below Mount Hermon in the north.

f.g: “The bald mountain,” in the Negev.
The mountains of Edom.

n: These victories took a long time — probably several years. The stories in Joshua compress a lengthy campaign.

f.g: Caleb’s age suggests about seven years.

n: Only Gibeon made peace; every other city fought and was taken in battle.

f.w: save the Hivites the inhabitants of Gibeon

n: The Canaanites’ hearts were hardened so they chose war rather than peace. As with Pharaoh, scripture describes God’s judgment working through people’s own stubborn choices.

f.w: that they might have no favour
f.g: That they would receive no mercy.

n: Joshua also defeated the Anakim — a people remembered as giants who had terrified the earlier spies — in the hill country.

f.g: Descendants of Anak, a tall people.

n: Some Anakim survived in the Philistine cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. Goliath of Gath may have descended from them.
The summary: Joshua took the land and divided it among the tribes, and the land rested from war. This prepares for the land allotments that follow.

f.w: according to their divisions by their tribes
